doc_description: Corning Incorporated’s 2022 Form 10-K (NYSE: GLW; File No. 1-3247) provides a comprehensive overview of its five reportable segments plus Hemlock Semiconductor, 2022 performance ($14.2B net sales; record $5B in Optical Communications), global footprint (124 plants in 15 countries), extensive IP, key risks, liquidity and capital actions, market risk disclosures, governance, and exhibits.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC filing overview: Corning Incorporated’s Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, Commission File No. 1-3247; common stock listed on NYSE (GLW).
- Company identifiers: New York corporation; EIN 16-0393470; principal office at One Riverfront Plaza, Corning, NY 14831; phone 607-974-9000.
- Registrant status and compliance: well-known seasoned issuer; current with Exchange Act filings and Interactive Data submissions; large accelerated filer; not an emerging growth or smaller reporting company; auditor attestation of internal control under SOX 404(b); not a shell company.
- Market data and share count: non-affiliate market value approx. $26 billion as of June 30, 2022; 846,563,422 shares outstanding as of January 31, 2023.
- Incorporation by reference: portions of the definitive Proxy Statement for the April 27, 2023 Annual Meeting are incorporated into Part III.
- Forward-looking statements: cautionary note highlighting risks and uncertainties, with references to Risk Factors and MD&A.
- Item 1. Business – General:
  - Heritage and corporate history: origins in 1851; incorporated in 1936; name changed from Corning Glass Works to Corning Incorporated in 1989.
  - Strategy and capabilities: focus on glass science, ceramic science, optical physics, and advanced manufacturing/engineering; strong R&D investment; partnership approach to solving customer challenges.
  - Markets served: optical communications, mobile consumer electronics, display technology, automotive emissions control, laboratory products, and other glass products.
  - Key products: damage-resistant cover glass; precision display glass; optical fiber, cable, wireless technologies, and connectivity solutions; life sciences tools for drug discovery/delivery; clean-air technologies for vehicles.
  - Global footprint: manufacturing at 124 plants in 15 countries.
  - Reportable segments: Optical Communications, Display Technologies, Specialty Materials, Environmental Technologies, and Life Sciences.
- Optical Communications segment details:
  - Innovation legacy: invented first low-loss optical fiber in 1970; ongoing leadership in fiber, cable, and connectivity.
  - Market drivers: exponential video-driven data growth; industry migration from copper to optical to meet capacity cost-effectively.
  - Solutions scope: designs delivering optical connectivity to the network edge.
  - Product groupings:
    - Carrier network: optical infrastructure for video, data, and voice services.
    - Enterprise network: optical networks sold to businesses, governments, and individuals for private use.

nodes.summary: Part I of Corning Incorporated’s report introduces the company and includes a forward-looking statements disclaimer noting potential risks and uncertainties referenced elsewhere in the filing. Item 1 (Business) provides general background: Corning’s origins (1851), incorporation (1936), and name change (1989); its mission and core strengths in glass science, ceramic science, optical physics, and advanced manufacturing; and its role in enabling multiple industries. It outlines key markets (optical communications, mobile consumer electronics, display technology, automotive emissions control, laboratory products, and other glass products) and flagship product categories (damage‑resistant cover glass, precision display glass, optical fiber/cable and connectivity, life sciences tools, and clean‑air technologies). The company’s global footprint includes 124 manufacturing plants in 15 countries and five reportable segments: Optical Communications, Display Technologies, Specialty Materials, Environmental Technologies, and Life Sciences. The section then details the Optical Communications segment, noting Corning’s invention of the first low‑loss optical fiber (1970), continued leadership amid rising data/video demand and the shift from copper to optical networks, and the segment’s two product groupings: carrier network solutions for service providers and enterprise network solutions for businesses, governments, and individuals.

nodes.title: Optical Communications Segment
nodes.heading: Optical Communications Segment
nodes.start_phrase: We invented the world’s first low-loss optical fiber in 1970.
nodes.summary:
- Part I of Corning Incorporated’s report, opening with standard forward-looking statements cautioning about risks and uncertainties and referencing sections like Risk Factors and MD&A.
- Item 1. Business: Company background and identity—origins in 1851, incorporated in 1936 in New York, name change to Corning Incorporated in 1989.
- Overview of Corning’s mission and core competencies in glass science, ceramic science, and optical physics; emphasis on R&D, engineering, and manufacturing scale enabling innovation across multiple industries.
- Markets served: optical communications, mobile consumer electronics, display technology, automotive emissions control, laboratory products, and other glass products.
- Examples of leading products: damage-resistant cover glass, precision display glass, optical fiber/cable and connectivity for networks, life sciences lab products, and clean-air technologies.
- Global footprint: 124 manufacturing plants in 15 countries; operations organized into five reportable segments—Optical Communications, Display Technologies, Specialty Materials, Environmental Technologies, and Life Sciences.
- Optical Communications segment:
  - Structure: carrier network and enterprise network.
  - Carrier portfolio: broad range of optical fibers (e.g., Vascade, LEAF, SMF-28 family including Ultra and Contour, ClearCurve), cables (RocketRibbon, miniXtend) for outdoor/indoor and 5G applications, and hardware/equipment (assemblies, connectors, components, closures) offered as components or integrated solutions (Evolv for fiber-to-the-home/5G, Centrix for high-density fiber management). Includes select copper-based products.
  - Enterprise portfolio: optical solutions for data centers and enterprises, including ClearCurve multimode fiber and integrated platforms (EDGE for high-density data centers up to 400G+, Everon for indoor cellular).
  - Manufacturing: fiber in North Carolina, China, India, and Poland; cabling in North Carolina, Poland, and regional sites; hardware/equipment in Texas, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, Poland, and China.
  - Intellectual property: extensive patent portfolio and select inbound/outbound licensing; royalties not material.
  - Financial note: segment represented 34% of total segment net sales in 2022.
- Display Technologies segment:
  - Focus: glass substrates for LCD and OLED displays used in TVs, notebooks, monitors, tablets, and handheld devices.
  - Technology: proprietary fusion manufacturing process delivering pristine surfaces, thermal stability, and dimensional uniformity; scalable and cost-effective for large-size substrates.

nodes.title: Display Technologies Segment
nodes.heading: Display Technologies Segment
nodes.start_phrase: The Display Technologies segment manufactures glass substrates for flat panel displays, including liquid crystal displays (“LCDs”) and organic light-emitting diodes (“OLEDs”) that are used primarily in televisions, notebook computers, desktop monitors, tablets and handheld devices.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Corning’s Optical Communications (carrier and enterprise) portfolios, highlighting a broad range of optical fibers (Vascade for submarine; LEAF for long-haul/metro; SMF-28 ULL/TXF for scalable long-haul/regional; SMF-28e+ for added metro/access wavelengths; ClearCurve ultra-bendable for MDU/FTTH; SMF-28 Ultra and SMF-28 Contour for low attenuation and macrobend performance), cable products (RocketRibbon, miniXtend for outdoor/indoor/5G), and hardware/equipment (cable assemblies, connectors, components, closures, NIDs). Notes integrated solutions such as Evolv (pre-connectorized FTTH/5G), Centrix (high-density fiber management), EDGE (high-density data center cabling to 400G+), and Everon (indoor cellular connectivity). Mentions select copper-based offerings (subscriber demarcation, xDSL passive solutions, outside plant enclosures).
- Outlines manufacturing footprint: optical fiber in North Carolina, China, India, and a new Poland facility (Q3 2022); cabling in North Carolina, Poland, and regional sites; hardware/equipment in Texas, Mexico, Brazil, Germany, Poland, and China.
- Notes IP importance and patent licensing (with royalty income not currently material) and use of third-party patents. Optical Communications represented 34% of 2022 segment net sales.
- Details the Display Technologies segment: glass substrates for LCD and OLED displays (TVs, notebooks, monitors, tablets, handhelds), produced via Corning’s proprietary fusion process enabling pristine surfaces, thermal stability, dimensional uniformity, scalability, and cost efficiency for large substrates. Highlights innovations including EAGLE XG Slim Glass (>30B sq ft sold), Astra Glass (optimized for oxide TFT, spanning a-Si to LTPS), Lotus NXT (for high-resolution, smaller/flexible devices), and first Gen 10/10.5 substrate sizes. Manufacturing in China, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan. IP and trade secrets are critical. Segment was 22% of 2022 net sales.
- Covers the Specialty Materials segment: 150+ formulations for glass/glass-ceramics/crystals and precision metrology across mobile electronics, semiconductor equipment, aerospace/defense, radiation shielding, sunglasses, and telecom. Features Gorilla Glass (including Victus 2 with better concrete-drop resistance and strong scratch resistance) made in the U.S., South Korea, and Taiwan; Ceramic Shield (co-developed with Apple) for iPhone front covers; semiconductor optics (HPFS fused silica, ULE glass), metrology instruments, and custom assemblies made in New York; ultra-flat/ultra-thin wafers/substrates for AR, advanced packaging, and 3D sensing made in New York, France, and China; sunglasses and radiation shielding made in France. Emphasizes patents/trademarks. Segment was 14% of 2022 net sales.

nodes.title: Specialty Materials Segment
nodes.heading: Specialty Materials Segment
nodes.start_phrase: The Specialty Materials segment manufactures products that provide more than 150 material formulations for glass, glass ceramics and crystals, as well as precision metrology instruments and software to meet requirements for unique customer needs.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Corning’s leadership in precision glass innovations, especially for larger, thinner, flexible, high-resolution displays.
- Display Technologies segment:
  - Key products: Corning EAGLE XG Slim Glass, Astra Glass, Lotus NXT Glass, and Gen 10/10.5 glass substrates.
  - Manufacturing in China, South Korea, Japan, and Taiwan; strong IP protection.
  - Accounted for 22% of 2022 segment net sales.
- Specialty Materials segment:
  - Broad portfolio of glass, glass-ceramics, crystals, and precision metrology for diverse markets (mobile electronics, semiconductor optics, aerospace/defense, radiation shielding, sunglasses, telecom components).
  - Flagship products: Corning Gorilla Glass (including Victus 2), Ceramic Shield (developed with Apple), semiconductor optics (HPFS Fused Silica, ULE Ultra-Low Expansion Glass), ultra-thin/flat glass wafers for AR and advanced packaging.
  - Manufacturing in the U.S., South Korea, Taiwan, France, and China; strong patents and trademarks.
  - Accounted for 14% of 2022 segment net sales.
- Environmental Technologies segment:
  - Ceramic substrates and filters for vehicle emissions control; innovations include FLORA substrates and DuraTrap GC gasoline particulate filters.
  - Manufacturing in New York, Virginia, China, and Germany; sold primarily to emission control system manufacturers per OEM specs; robust IP portfolio.
  - Accounted for 11% of 2022 segment net sales.
- Life Sciences segment:
  - Lab consumables, specialty surfaces, media/serum, labware, and equipment for drug discovery, diagnostics, advanced cell culture, genomics, and bioproduction.
  - Brands: Corning, Falcon, PYREX, Axygen; global distribution to pharma, biotech, CMOs, labs, academia, hospitals, and governments.
  - Manufacturing across multiple U.S. states and in China, France, Mexico, Brazil, and Poland; strong IP and brand focus.
  - Accounted for 8% of 2022 segment net sales.
- Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses:
  - Consolidated results from Hemlock Semiconductor Group since 2020.
  - HSG provides high-purity polysilicon for solar power and electronics (semiconductor wafers and integrated circuits).

nodes.title: Environmental Technologies Segment
nodes.heading: Environmental Technologies Segment
nodes.start_phrase: The Environmental Technologies segment manufactures ceramic substrates and filter products for emissions control in mobile applications around the world.
nodes.summary:
- Environmental Technologies segment: Manufactures ceramic substrates and filter products for global automotive emissions control; pioneered cellular ceramic substrates in the 1970s and continues innovation with low-mass Corning FLORA substrates and Corning DuraTrap GC gasoline particulate filters. Production in New York, Virginia, China, and Germany. Sells primarily to emission-control system manufacturers specified by automotive and engine OEMs. Strong patent portfolio and key licenses support operations. Contributed 11% of Corning’s 2022 segment net sales.

- Life Sciences segment: Longstanding supplier (105+ years) of laboratory products enabling research and bioproduction across small molecules, biologics, vaccines, and cell/gene therapies. Products include consumables (plastic vessels, liquid handling, specialty surfaces, cell culture media/serum), general labware, glassware, and equipment used in drug discovery, screening, diagnostics, advanced cell culture, genomics, and cell mass production. Marketed globally under Corning, Falcon, PYREX, and Axygen brands via distributors to pharma, biotech, CMOs, testing labs, academia, hospitals, and government. Manufacturing footprint spans multiple U.S. states and countries (including China, France, Mexico, Brazil, Poland). Patents and trademark-driven brand equity are important. Contributed 8% of 2022 segment net sales.

- Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses: Aggregates businesses below reporting thresholds, primarily Hemlock Semiconductor Group (HSG), consolidated since gaining control in Q3 2020 (Sept 9, 2020). HSG supplies high-purity polysilicon to solar and electronics markets, serving solar cell/panel production and semiconductor wafer/integrated circuit manufacturing. References provided to financial note on HSG transactions and acquisitions.

nodes.title: Life Sciences Segment
nodes.heading: Life Sciences Segment
nodes.start_phrase: As a leading developer, manufacturer and global supplier of laboratory products for over 105 years, the Life Sciences segment works with researchers and drug manufacturers seeking to drive innovation, increase efficiencies, reduce costs and compress timelines.
nodes.summary:
- Environmental Technologies segment: Manufactures ceramic substrates and filter products for global mobile emissions control; long history of innovation since the 1970s, including low-mass Corning FLORA substrates and Corning DuraTrap GC gasoline particulate filters; manufactures in New York, Virginia, China and Germany; sells primarily to catalyzers and emission control system manufacturers whose products are specified by auto and diesel OEMs; relies on a broad patent portfolio and certain licensed patents; accounted for 11% of Corning’s 2022 segment net sales.

- Life Sciences segment: Longstanding global supplier of lab products supporting research, drug development and bioproduction; leverages expertise in materials science, polymer surface science, cell culture and cell biology; offerings include consumables (vessels, liquid handling plastics, specialty surfaces, media, serum), general labware, glassware and equipment; used in drug discovery, screening, diagnostics, advanced cell culture, genomics and cell mass production; sold under Corning, Falcon, PYREX and Axygen brands, primarily through distributors to pharma, biotech, CMOs, testing labs, academia, hospitals and governments; manufactures across multiple U.S. states and in China, France, Mexico, Brazil and Poland; emphasizes patents and brand strength; represented 8% of 2022 segment net sales.

- Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses: Aggregates businesses below reporting thresholds, principally Hemlock Semiconductor Group (HSG); Corning obtained a controlling interest in Q3 2020 and consolidated results beginning September 9, 2020; HSG is a leading producer of high-purity polysilicon for solar power and electronics, supporting solar cell/panel/array manufacturing and semiconductor wafers/integrated circuits; references provided to related financial statement notes and the Patents and Trademarks section.

nodes.title: Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses
nodes.heading: Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses
nodes.start_phrase: All other businesses that do not meet the quantitative threshold for separate reporting have been grouped as Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses.
nodes.summary:
- Describes Corning’s Environmental Technologies segment, which manufactures ceramic substrates and filters for vehicle emissions control. Highlights its pioneering cellular ceramic substrate from the 1970s, continued innovation (e.g., low-mass Corning FLORA substrates and DuraTrap GC gasoline particulate filters), global manufacturing in the U.S., China, and Germany, sales to emission control system makers per automaker specifications, the importance of patent protection, and that the segment accounted for 11% of 2022 segment net sales.

- Details the Life Sciences segment as a long-standing global supplier of lab products supporting drug discovery through bioproduction. Covers key products (plastic consumables, specialty surfaces, media and serum, labware, equipment), applications (R&D, diagnostics, genomics, cell production), major brands (Corning, Falcon, PYREX, Axygen), distribution primarily through global distributors to pharma, biotech, CMOs, labs, academia, hospitals, and governments, extensive global manufacturing footprint, the importance of patents and trademarks, and that it represented 8% of 2022 segment net sales.

- Explains Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses, primarily comprising Hemlock Semiconductor Group (consolidated since September 9, 2020), a leading provider of high-purity polysilicon for solar and electronics. Also includes pharmaceutical technologies (glass tubing and vials), automotive glass solutions (lightweight, damage-resistant windows and displays), and other businesses and investments. This group represented 11% of 2022 segment net sales. References to MD&A and Note 19 for further segment and geographic information.

- Outlines competition: Corning faces numerous global competitors, some larger or with broader product lines, and seeks advantage through R&D, customer relationships, reliable supply, quality, service, and technical specifications. Provides segment-specific competitive landscapes and key rivals:
  - Optical Communications: leadership in carrier and enterprise networks; ongoing consolidation and pricing pressure; advantages in large-scale manufacturing, fiber process, technology, and IP; competitors include CommScope and Prysmian.
  - Display Technologies: largest producer of glass substrates for flat panel displays; advantages from the proprietary fusion process yielding large, thin, light, high-quality glass without heavy metals; competitors include AGC and Nippon Electric Glass.
  - Specialty Materials: broad materials and optical capabilities serving semiconductor, aerospace, defense, industrial, commercial, and telecom; competitors include Schott, AGC, Nippon Electric Glass, and Heraeus.
  - Environmental Technologies: strong position in automotive ceramic substrates and filters for emissions; advantages include product portfolio, collaborative engineering, service/support, global presence, and innovation; competitors include NGK Insulators and Ibiden.
  - Life Sciences: competes on quality, global distribution, supply chain efficiency, breadth, technical support, and product attributes; competitors include Thermo Fisher, Avantor, Greiner, Eppendorf, Sarstedt, and Danaher, with additional competition from distributors pursuing private labels or backward integration.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.heading: Competition
nodes.start_phrase: We compete with many large and varied manufacturers, both domestic and foreign.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses: Includes pharmaceutical technologies (glass tubing and vials for pharma), automotive glass solutions (lightweight, damage‑resistant windows and displays), plus other businesses and certain corporate investments; represented 11% of Corning’s total segment net sales in 2022. Additional segment and geographic details are referenced in MD&A and Note 19 (Reportable Segments).

- Companywide competition: Corning faces numerous domestic and foreign competitors, some larger or with broader product lines. The company emphasizes R&D, deep customer relationships, reliable supply, product quality, superior service, and technical product specifications to sustain competitive advantage, though no assurance of maintaining position is given.

- Optical Communications: Maintains leadership in carrier and enterprise networks amid consolidation, pricing pressure, and innovation competition; advantages include large-scale manufacturing, fiber process, technology leadership, and IP. Key competitors: CommScope, Prysmian.

- Display Technologies: Largest global producer of glass substrates for flat panel displays; edge maintained through investment in new products, proprietary fusion manufacturing, and reliable high-quality supply. Glass is larger, thinner, lighter, with exceptional surface quality and no heavy metals. Key competitors: AGC, Nippon Electric Glass.

- Specialty Materials: Broad capabilities in materials science and optics (design, shaping, coating, finishing, metrology, assembly) serving semiconductor, aerospace, defense, industrial, commercial, and telecom markets. Key competitors: Schott, AGC, Nippon Electric Glass, Heraeus.

- Environmental Technologies: Strong global position in automotive ceramic substrates and filters for catalytic converters and particulate emissions, including heavy-duty and light-duty diesel markets; advantages include product portfolio, collaborative engineering, customer support, global presence, and ongoing innovation. Key competitors: NGK Insulators, Ibiden.

- Life Sciences: Competes on product quality, global distribution, supply chain efficiency, breadth of line, technical support, and superior attributes; faces competition from major brands and from distributors pursuing backward integration or private labels. Key competitors: Thermo Fisher Scientific, Avantor, Greiner, Eppendorf, Sarstedt, Danaher.

The company enforces its IP, views the portfolio as a competitive advantage, and notes competitors also actively patent; no single patent is material.

nodes.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
nodes.start_phrase: The following Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations (“MD&A”) was prepared to provide a historical and prospective narrative on our financial condition and results of operations through the eyes of management and should be read in conjunction with our consolidated financial statements and the accompanying notes to those financial statements.
nodes.summary:
- Document scope: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) for financial condition and results of operations, to be read with consolidated financial statements; 2021–2020 comparisons are excluded and referenced to the 2021 Form 10-K.
- MD&A structure: Overview; Results of Operations; Segment Analysis; Core Performance Measures; Liquidity and Capital Resources; Environment; Critical Accounting Estimates; New Accounting Standards; Forward-Looking Statements.
- Strategy & growth framework (2020–2023): Focus on selling more Corning content across Market-Access Platforms; target core sales CAGR of 6–8%; achieved >8% core sales CAGR from 2019–2022 despite external headwinds.
- Key strategic advancements by business:
  - Optical Communications: fiber-to-the-home and data center solutions; record $5B sales in 2022.
  - Environmental Technologies: delivered gasoline particulate filter content opportunity.
  - Specialty Materials: introduced Ceramic Shield with Apple.
  - Display Technologies: ramped Gen 10.5 plants to extend leadership.
  - Emerging innovations: traction in Automotive Glass Solutions.
  - Pharmaceutical packaging: pivotal in COVID-19 response, supporting delivery of 8+ billion doses.
- Operating environment since 2020: pandemic-driven disruptions, supply chain issues, variable consumer spending, and inflation; 2022 performance outpaced consumer-facing end markets and captured growth in solar.
- Profitability and cash flow: lagged sales due to elevated staffing, higher-than-normal inventories, and persistent inflation affecting materials, production, shipping, and inventory costs.
- Actions taken in 2022 (especially Q4): price increases to share inflation with customers; productivity adjustments toward historical ratios without impairing supply or growth; normalization of inventory levels.
- Outlook: continue disciplined operations, adapt to current conditions, and advance growth initiatives; portfolio seen as strategically resilient; confidence in durable multiyear growth with improved margins and cash generation.

nodes.start_phrase: We introduced our 2020-to-2023 Strategy & Growth Framework with a focus on capturing opportunities to sell more Corning content through each of our Market-Access Platforms.

(Comparisons of 2021 vs. 2020 are referenced to the 2021 Form 10-K.)
- Strategy update: 2020–2023 Strategy & Growth Framework aimed at selling more Corning content via Market-Access Platforms, targeting 6–8% core sales CAGR; achieved >8% CAGR from 2019–2022.
- Strategic achievements: expansion in fiber-to-the-home and data center (Optical Communications); delivery of gasoline particulate filter content (Environmental Technologies); launch of Ceramic Shield with Apple (Specialty Materials); Gen 10.5 ramp to extend leadership (Display Technologies); progress in Automotive Glass Solutions; pharma packaging supported >8 billion COVID-19 doses; momentum in emerging innovations.
- Operating environment since 2020: pandemic impacts including supply chain disruptions, productivity challenges, consumer spending swings, and inflation. In 2022, the company outperformed consumer-facing end markets, captured solar growth, and achieved record $5B Optical Communications sales.
- Profitability/cash flow pressures despite sales growth due to elevated staffing, higher inventory levels, and inflation in materials, production, shipping, and inventory carrying costs.
- 2022 actions to improve profitability and cash: price increases to share inflation with customers; productivity ratio adjustments toward historical levels; inventory normalization (notably in Q4).
- Ongoing focus on disciplined operations and advancing growth initiatives; confidence in durable multiyear growth with improving margins and cash generation.
- 2022 financial results: net sales $14.2B (+1% YoY). Growth in Optical Communications (+$674M, +15%) and Hemlock & Emerging Growth Businesses (+$419M, +34%) offset decline in Display Technologies (−$394M). Foreign exchange reduced consolidated net sales by $616M.

  - Total translated earnings contract gain, net, was essentially flat year over year (2022: $351m pre-tax, $269m net; 2021: $354m pre-tax, $273m net).

- Discusses the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022: a 15% book minimum tax applicable starting in 2024; not expected to materially affect the company’s effective tax rate; evaluating available credits and overall impact.

nodes.title: Provision for Income Taxes

nodes.start_phrase: For the year ended December 31, 2022, the effective tax rate differed from the U.S. statutory rate of 21% primarily due to the following:

- The section explains Corning’s translated earnings contracts, which economically hedge translation exposure in JPY, KRW, TWD, EUR, CNY, and GBP, and their effect on net income.

Realized gains increased significantly in 2022 ($320 million pre-tax/$245 million net vs. $47 million/$36 million in 2021), while unrealized gains decreased ($31 million/$24 million vs. $307 million/$237 million in 2021). 2022 included $20 million of pre-tax realized gains from option expirations vs. $20 million pre-tax realized losses in 2021. Unrealized impacts were primarily driven by JPY, KRW, and EUR-denominated hedges.
- Foreign currency translation, including hedges realized in the year, adversely impacted income before income taxes by $142 million in 2022 compared to 2021.
- Provision for income taxes: 
  - 2022 effective tax rate differences from the 21% U.S. statutory rate were driven by net provisions for tax reserves ($67 million), foreign earnings ($40 million), and valuation allowance changes ($38 million), partially offset by tax credits ($60 million) and FDII benefits ($49 million).

- Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of 2022: a 15% book minimum tax will apply beginning in 2024; Corning does not expect a material impact on its effective tax rate and is evaluating available credits.
- Net income attributable to Corning Incorporated was $1,316 million in 2022 vs. $1,906 million in 2021. After reflecting 2021 preferred stock items (a $24 million dividend and $803 million excess consideration for redemption tied to Samsung Display Co., Ltd.), net income available to common shareholders used for EPS was $1,316 million (2022) vs. $1,079 million (2021). EPS: basic $1.56 vs. $1.30; diluted $1.54 vs. $1.28. Weighted-average shares: basic 843 million vs. 828 million; diluted 857 million vs. 844 million.
- Comprehensive income attributable to Corning decreased by $810 million, primarily due to a $549 million decline in net income and a $175 million increase in net foreign currency translation losses, mainly from JPY, CNY, and KRW.

nodes.title: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES
nodes.heading: CRITICAL ACCOUNTING ESTIMATES
nodes.start_phrase: Our consolidated financial statements are prepared in conformity with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America.
nodes.summary:
- Describes management’s critical accounting estimates under US GAAP and their potential material impact on results, financial position, and cash flows.
- Details the valuation of a previously held equity interest upon gaining control of HSG using the acquisition method, including fair value measurements of identifiable assets (intangible assets, fixed assets, inventories) and liabilities (contract liabilities, debt). Notes a measurement period of up to one year with offsetting goodwill adjustments for refinements.
- Reports a September 2020 event in which HSG redeemed DuPont’s ownership for $250 million, leading to a recognized pre-tax gain of $498 million on the previously held equity interest, derived from the difference between fair value and carrying value. - Explains the impairment assessment of long-lived assets, performed quarterly upon indicators of impairment, with specific discussion of precious metals (platinum, rhodium) embedded in manufacturing equipment: not depreciated due to long useful life and low physical loss; physical losses expensed as depletion; metals reviewed for impairment whether in use, in reclamation/fabrication/refinement, or awaiting deployment, and held only to support operations.
- Lists example impairment indicators: significant market price declines; changes in use or physical condition; adverse legal or business climate developments (including regulatory actions); significant cost overruns; recurring or forecasted operating/cash flow losses; and expectations of early sale or disposal before the end of useful life.

nodes.title: Valuation of the Previously Held Equity Interest from the Consolidation of HSG
nodes.heading: Valuation of the Previously Held Equity Interest from the Consolidation of HSG
nodes.start_phrase: We account for the change in controlling interest using the acquisition method of accounting, which requires us to estimate the fair values of the assets and liabilities recorded.
nodes.summary:
- Focus of the section: Critical accounting estimates that require significant management judgment and could materially affect results, financial position, and cash flows.
- Valuation of previously held equity interest from HSG consolidation:
  - Change in control accounted for under the acquisition method; fair values estimated for acquired assets (e.g., developed technology, know‑how, tradenames, customer intangibles, fixed assets, inventory) and assumed liabilities (e.g., customer deposits, deferred revenue, debt).
  - Any gain or loss from remeasurement recognized in earnings; measurement period of up to one year may lead to adjustments to provisional amounts, with offsetting changes to goodwill.
  - Estimates rely on acceptable valuation models, independent appraisals, and management assumptions; differences between estimated and actual outcomes can impact reported results.
  - September 2020 event: HSG redeemed DuPont’s interest for $250 million, triggering consolidation and a recognized pre‑tax gain of $498 million on the previously held equity interest, measured as the difference between fair value and carrying value. Fair value estimated using an income approach with key assumptions including projected revenue, a 16.5% discount rate, and a 0% terminal growth rate.
- Impairment of assets held for use:
  - Quarterly assessment for indicators of impairment of long‑lived assets, requiring judgment.
  - Special treatment of precious metals (platinum, rhodium) used in manufacturing equipment: not depreciated due to very long useful life and minimal physical loss; physical loss recognized as depletion expense based on actual units lost; metals reviewed for impairment and tracked whether in production, reclamation, fabrication/refinement, or awaiting use; not held for trading.
  - Examples of impairment indicators include: significant market price declines; significant changes in asset use or condition; adverse legal or business climate (including regulatory actions); substantial cost overruns; ongoing or forecasted operating/cash flow losses; expectation of early sale or disposal versus original useful life.

nodes.title: Impairment of assets held for use
nodes.heading: Impairment of assets held for use
nodes.start_phrase: We are required to assess the recoverability of the carrying value of long-lived assets when an indicator of impairment has been identified.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of critical accounting estimates under U.S. GAAP, emphasizing management judgment and potential material impacts on results, position, and cash flows.
- Valuation of previously held equity interest from consolidation of HSG:
  - Acquisition method applied at change in control with fair value estimates for acquired assets (intangibles, fixed assets, inventory) and liabilities (deferred revenue, debt).
  - Measurement-period adjustments may affect goodwill.
  - September 2020 HSG Redemption led to consolidation and a $498 million pre-tax gain from remeasuring the equity method investment to fair value.
  - Fair value determined primarily via an income approach using key assumptions (projected revenue, 16.5% discount rate, 0% terminal growth) supported by independent appraisals.
- Impairment of long-lived assets held for use:
  - Quarterly review for impairment indicators and judgment in defining asset groups at the lowest level of largely independent cash flows (often across locations sharing supply chains within operating segments).
  - Treatment of precious metals in manufacturing equipment (platinum, rhodium): not depreciated; physical losses recognized as depletion expense; included in impairment assessments.
  - Examples of impairment indicators (market price declines, adverse legal/business changes, cost overruns, operating losses, early disposal expectations).
  - Recoverability test based on undiscounted cash flows including disposition; if failed, fair value measured via income approach, considering precious metals and market conditions; sensitivity primarily to market growth, volume, and pricing assumptions.
  - 2020 example: $217 million pre-tax impairment and disposal loss tied to discontinuation of certain R&D programs within Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses; fair value measured with Level 3 inputs.
- Income taxes:
  - Assessment of deferred tax asset realizability requires estimates of future taxable income and tax planning strategies.
  - Accounting for uncertain tax positions under ASC 740 using the “more-likely-than-not” threshold and measurement based on expected sustained benefit; judgments may change as new information emerges.

nodes.title: Income taxes
nodes.heading: Income taxes
nodes.start_phrase: We are required to exercise judgment about our future results in assessing the realizability of our deferred tax assets.
nodes.summary:
- Impairment of long‑lived assets: how asset groups are identified at the lowest level of largely independent cash flows (assessed at the operating segment level and often combined across locations sharing supply chains); recoverability testing using undiscounted future cash flows including disposition; considerations of asset utilization and idled capacity; fair value measurement via an income approach (including precious metals where applicable); key sensitivities (market growth, volumes, selling prices) and reliance on Level 3 inputs when necessary.
- 2020 impairment event: discontinuation of certain R&D programs within Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses led to an asset group impairment and disposal loss totaling $217 million pre‑tax (nearly all carrying value, including an insignificant amount of goodwill), with fair value measured using unobservable Level 3 inputs; cross‑reference to Note 2.
- Income taxes: judgments in assessing realizability of deferred tax assets based on forecasts of future taxable income and tax planning strategies; accounting for uncertain tax positions under ASC 740, recognizing benefits only when more likely than not, and adjusting as new information arises.
- Fair value measures: use of observable and unobservable inputs classified into a three‑level hierarchy; application of highest‑and‑best‑use for non‑financial assets; major categories measured at fair value include investments, certain pension assets, and derivatives, generally using market approaches and observable inputs.
- Derivatives and hedging: valuation of interest rate swaps and foreign exchange forwards; FX hedges for yen, won, euro, NT dollar, yuan, and pound; accounting for cash flow hedges through AOCI with reclassification to earnings when hedged items affect results; non‑designated contracts recognized in earnings; credit risk adjustments deemed immaterial; cross‑reference to Note 15.
- Litigation: estimation of probable outcomes based on counsel evaluations, case law, and matter specifics; references to Item 3 and Note 13 for material proceedings.
- Pension and OPEB: benefit cost and obligation drivers (discount rates, expected returns, compensation growth, health care trend, and demographics); defined benefit pension cost components (ongoing quarterly costs and annual mark‑to‑market outside a 10% corridor, with interim remeasurements when triggered); OPEB cost components and recognition of actuarial gains/losses in AOCI with amortization over employees’ average remaining service period.

nodes.title: Fair value measures
nodes.heading: Fair value measures
nodes.start_phrase: As required, we use two kinds of inputs to determine the fair value of assets and liabilities: observable and unobservable.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines the company’s fair value measurement framework, distinguishing observable versus unobservable inputs and prioritizing them within a three-level hierarchy. Emphasizes use of observable market data and a market approach for major categories (short- and long-term investments, certain pension assets, and derivatives).
- Describes derivative valuation and hedge accounting: interest rate swaps and FX forwards measured using observable prices for similar instruments; FX hedges address exposure to JPY, KRW, EUR, TWD, CNY, and GBP. Cash flow hedge fair value changes go to accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI) and are reclassified to income when the hedged item affects earnings; non-designated derivatives flow through earnings. Credit risk considerations are included and deemed immaterial. References Note 15 for more detail.
- Explains the approach to estimating probabilities of litigation outcomes, relying on counsel evaluations, case law, and case specifics; directs readers to Item 3 and Note 13 for material matters.
- Details accounting for defined benefit pensions and other postretirement employee benefits (OPEB), including key economic and demographic assumptions (interest rates, expected asset returns, compensation growth, health care trend, retirements/mortality/turnover/participation) and their potential impact on obligations and expense.
- For pensions: identifies ongoing quarterly costs (service cost, interest cost, expected return on assets, amortization of prior service cost) and annual fourth-quarter mark-to-market recognition of gains/losses outside a 10% corridor of the greater of the benefit obligation or market-related asset value; interim remeasurements (e.g., curtailments, settlements, significant plan changes) recognized when they occur.
- For OPEB: notes ongoing quarterly costs (service and interest) plus amortization of prior service and actuarial gains/losses; actuarial gains/losses recognized in AOCI annually and amortized into results over the average remaining service period to the extent outside the corridor.

nodes.title: Probability of litigation outcomes
nodes.heading: Probability of litigation outcomes
nodes.start_phrase: We are required to make judgments about future events that are inherently uncertain.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the fair value measurement framework, distinguishing observable vs. unobservable inputs, prioritizing inputs into a three-level hierarchy, requiring use of observable market data when available, and applying highest-and-best-use for non-financial assets.
- Identifies major categories measured at fair value—short- and long-term investments, certain pension asset investments, and derivatives—valued primarily using market approaches with quoted prices in active or less active markets.
- Describes derivative instruments (interest rate swaps and foreign currency forwards) and related hedge activities across multiple currencies (JPY, KRW, EUR, TWD, CNY, GBP), including accounting: cash flow hedges recorded in AOCI and reclassified to earnings, non-designated hedges recognized in earnings; credit risk effects deemed immaterial; references Note 15 for details.
- Outlines the approach to estimating litigation outcomes, relying on counsel evaluation, case law, and case specifics; directs readers to Item 3 Legal Proceedings and Note 13 for material matters.
- Summarizes pension and OPEB offerings and the key economic and demographic assumptions (interest rates, expected asset returns, compensation growth, healthcare trend, mortality/turnover/participation) that drive obligations and expense, noting sensitivity to assumption changes.
- Details pension expense components: quarterly ongoing costs (service cost, interest cost, expected return on assets, amortization of prior service cost) and annual Q4 mark-to-market recognition of gains/losses outside a 10% corridor; interim remeasurements for curtailments, settlements, or significant plan changes recognized when they occur.
- Details OPEB expense components: quarterly ongoing costs (service and interest costs, amortization of prior service cost and actuarial gains/losses), with actuarial gains/losses recorded in AOCI annually and amortized into results over the average remaining service period when outside the corridor.

nodes.title: Pension and other postretirement employee benefits (“OPEB”)
nodes.heading: Pension and other postretirement employee benefits (“OPEB”)
nodes.start_phrase: We offer employee retirement plans consisting of defined benefit pension plans covering certain domestic and international employees and postretirement plans that provide health care and life insurance benefits for eligible retirees and dependents.
nodes.summary:
- Explains the company’s fair value measurement framework:
  - Distinguishes observable vs. unobservable inputs and the three-level hierarchy.
  - Emphasizes use of observable market data and highest-and-best-use for non-financial assets.
  - Major categories measured at fair value (using market approaches and observable inputs): short- and long-term investments, certain pension assets, and derivatives.
- Details on derivatives:
  - Types include interest rate swaps and FX forwards.
  - FX hedges cover JPY, KRW, EUR, TWD, CNY, and GBP.
  - Cash flow hedge accounting: changes recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI) and reclassified to income when hedged items affect earnings.
  - Non-designated hedges: fair value changes recognized in earnings (translated earnings contract gain/loss, net).
  - Credit risk considered in valuation; impacts not material.
  - References Note 15 for more information.
- Litigation contingencies:
  - Outcome judgments based on counsel evaluations, case law, and case specifics.
  - References Item 3 and Note 13 for material matters.
- Pension and OPEB accounting:
  - Describes defined benefit and retiree health/life plans and key economic/demographic assumptions (interest rates, expected returns, compensation growth, healthcare trends, mortality, turnover, participation).
  - Pension expense components: ongoing quarterly costs (service, interest, expected return, amortization) and annual Q4 mark-to-market outside the 10% corridor; interim remeasurements recognized when events occur.
  - OPEB expense: ongoing costs plus recognition of actuarial gains/losses in AOCI with amortization if outside corridor.
- Key figures and results:
  - 2022 saw significant negative actual returns on plan assets (Domestic: -20.05%; International: -26.26%) versus expected returns (Domestic: 6.00%; International: ~1.6%).
  - U.S. pension PBO at December 31, 2022: $3.2 billion.
- Sensitivity analyses:
  - U.S. pensions: 25 bp decrease in spot rates increases PBO by $74 million (ongoing expense -$1 million); 25 bp increase decreases PBO by $71 million (+$1 million to expense). A 25 bp change in expected return on assets changes ongoing expense by ±$7 million. No effect on funding requirements.
  - U.S. OPEB: 25 bp decrease in spot rates increases ongoing expense by $1 million and APBO by $12 million; 25 bp increase reduces them by $1 million and $11 million, respectively.
  - Notes that assumption changes are interrelated and effects are not necessarily linear.
- Notes adoption/disclosure references:
  - New accounting standards: see Note 1.
  - Additional details: see Notes 13 and 15.

nodes.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risks

nodes.start_phrase: We have audited the accompanying consolidated balance sheets of Corning Incorporated and its subsidiaries (the “Company”) as of December 31, 2022 and 2021, and the related consolidated statements of income, comprehensive income, changes in shareholders’ equity and cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended December 31, 2022, including the related notes (collectively referred to as the “consolidated financial statements”).

- Critical Audit Matter:
  - Income taxes – receivables related to South Korean tax disputes (2010–2018), including a $349 million non-current receivable recorded as of December 31, 2022.
  - Significant management judgment applying “more-likely-than-not” recognition; auditor procedures included control testing, evaluation of legal/technical positions, and use of tax specialists.

- Consolidated financial statements:
  - Statement of Income (2020–2022): 2022 net sales $14.2B; operating income $1.44B; net income $1.39B; net income attributable to Corning $1.32B; diluted EPS $1.54. Notes highlight translated earnings contract gains, interest expense, other income, and the impact of preferred stock dividends/redemption on net income available to common shareholders (notably in 2021).
  - Statement of Comprehensive Income: 2022 other comprehensive loss driven largely by foreign currency translation; comprehensive income attributable to Corning $661M.
  - Balance Sheet (12/31/22 vs. 12/31/21): total assets $29.5B; cash $1.67B; inventories $2.90B; PP&E (net) $15.37B; long-term debt $6.69B; total liabilities $17.22B; total equity $12.28B; increased accumulated other comprehensive loss.
  - Statement of Cash Flows: 2022 operating cash flow $2.62B; investing outflows primarily ~$1.6B capital expenditures; financing outflows include dividends ($932M), treasury stock purchases, debt activity, and preferred stock redemption payments; net decrease in cash to $1.67B.
  - Statement of Changes in Shareholders’ Equity: activity includes 2021 redemption and conversion of Series A convertible preferred stock, dividends, share issuances to benefit plans, treasury share repurchases, AOCI movements, and changes in non-controlling interests.

  - Hemlock Semiconductor Group: consolidation beginning September 9, 2020 following redemption of a prior owner’s interest; included within Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses.
  - Reclassifications to conform prior periods and the use of estimates across key areas (revenue recognition, restructuring, impairments, fair value, income taxes, pensions/OPEB, share-based compensation).

nodes.title: Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.heading: 1. Summary of Significant Accounting Policies
nodes.start_phrase: Corning Incorporated is a provider of high-performance glass for notebook computers, flat panel desktop monitors, display televisions and other information display applications; carrier network and enterprise network products for the telecommunications industry; ceramic substrates for gasoline and diesel engines in automotive and heavy-duty vehicle markets; laboratory products for the scientific community and specialized polymer products for biotechnology applications; advanced optical materials for the semiconductor industry and the scientific community; polycrystalline silicon products and other technologies.
nodes.summary:
- Section covered: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements—Summary of Significant Accounting Policies.
- Organization: Describes Corning’s businesses, including display glass; telecom carrier and enterprise network products; ceramic substrates for automotive and heavy-duty engines; laboratory and biotech polymer products; advanced optical materials for semiconductor/scientific uses; and polycrystalline silicon and related technologies. Defines terms used (“Corning,” “Company,” etc.).
- Basis of presentation and consolidation: Financials prepared under U.S. GAAP; intercompany items eliminated; equity method for investments where Corning has significant influence (typically >20%) without control; criteria for consolidating variable interest entities (VIEs) and disclosure that there were no material VIEs in the periods presented.
- HSG transaction: On Sept. 9, 2020, after Hemlock Semiconductor Group redeemed DuPont’s interest, Corning obtained 100% of HS LLC and 80.5% of HSO LLC; HSG has been consolidated since that date within Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses; reference to Note 3 for more details.
- Reclassifications: Certain prior-year amounts reclassified with no impact on results, position, or equity.
- Use of estimates: Management’s significant estimates affect revenue recognition, restructuring, impairment testing, fair value measurements (acquisitions, investments, equity interests), environmental and legal liabilities, income taxes and valuation allowances, pension/OPEB assumptions, and share-based compensation; actual results may differ from estimates.

nodes.summary:
