- Organization: Overview of Corning’s businesses, including display glass, telecom networks, automotive ceramic substrates, laboratory and biotech products, advanced optical materials, and polycrystalline silicon.
- Basis of presentation: Consolidation under U.S. GAAP; elimination of intercompany accounts and profits; equity method for investments where Corning has significant influence (generally >20% ownership); inclusion of affiliates’ earnings/losses in results.
- Variable interest entities (VIEs): Consolidation criteria outlined; no material consolidated or nonconsolidated VIEs during the periods presented.
- Hemlock Semiconductor Group (HSG) transaction: On Sept. 9, 2020, DuPont’s interest in HSG was redeemed for $250 million; Corning obtained 100% of HS LLC and 80.5% of HSO LLC; HSG has been consolidated since that date within Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses.
- Reclassifications: Certain prior-year amounts reclassified to conform to current presentation, with no impact on results, financial position, or equity.
- Use of estimates: Management’s significant estimates include revenue recognition, restructuring, goodwill and long-lived asset impairment, fair value of acquired assets/liabilities and investments, environmental and legal liabilities, income taxes and valuation allowances, pension/OPEB assumptions, and share-based compensation; actual results may differ from estimates.

nodes.title: Use of Estimates
nodes.heading: Use of Estimates
nodes.start_phrase: The preparation of financial statements, in conformity with GAAP, requires management to make estimates and assumptions affecting reported amounts of assets, liabilities, revenue, expenses and the disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities in the consolidated financial statements and related notes.
nodes.summary:
- Scope: Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements – Summary of Significant Accounting Policies for Corning Incorporated and subsidiaries.
- Organization: Overview of Corning’s diverse businesses (display glass, telecommunications networks, automotive ceramics, laboratory/biotech products, advanced optical materials, polycrystalline silicon and related technologies); definition of “Corning,” “Company,” etc.
- Basis of presentation and consolidation: Financials prepared under U.S. GAAP; elimination of intercompany transactions; equity method for significant influence investments (typically >20% ownership without control); VIE consolidation criteria and statement that there were no material VIEs in reported periods.
- Hemlock Semiconductor Group (HSG) transaction: On Sept. 9, 2020, DuPont’s interest in HSG was redeemed; Corning obtained 100% of HS LLC and 80.5% of HSO LLC; HSG consolidated thereafter within Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses; prior-period reclassifications made with no impact on results or equity.
- Use of estimates: Key areas include revenue recognition, restructuring, goodwill/long-lived asset impairment, fair value measurements (acquisitions, investments, equity interests), environmental/legal liabilities, income taxes and valuation allowances, pension/OPEB assumptions, and share-based compensation; outcomes may differ from estimates.
- Revenue recognition:
  - Products: Recognized at a point in time upon transfer of control; customer acceptance considered when applicable; shipping/handling treated as fulfillment costs; taxes excluded from revenue; returns/discounts/warranty allowances recorded based on history; warranty liabilities not material as of Dec. 31, 2022 and 2021.
  - Services/longer-term arrangements (mainly Telecommunications): Recognized over time using straight-line or input methods tied to effort/cost; other service revenue not material for 2020–2022.
- Contract assets and liabilities: Incremental costs to obtain/fulfill contracts are insignificant; most fulfillment costs captured in inventory, fixed, and intangible assets; contract liabilities include customer deposits (primarily Display) and deferred revenue (primarily HSG); other advance payments not significant and recorded in other accrued liabilities.
- Research and development: Expensed as incurred; totals were $0.9B (2022), $0.8B (2021), $1.0B (2020).
- Foreign currency: Functional currency generally local, with a notable exception of a Taiwanese subsidiary using Japanese yen; foreign currency remeasurement gains/losses recognized in income: +$130M (2022), +$126M (2021), −$37M (2020).

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition
nodes.heading: Revenue Recognition
nodes.start_phrase: Most of the Company’s revenue is generated by delivery of products to customers and recognized at a point in time based on evaluation of when the customer obtains control of the products.
nodes.summary:
- Covers Corning’s significant accounting policies focused on revenue recognition, contract assets and liabilities, research and development costs, and foreign currency translation.
- Revenue recognition:
  - Product sales recognized at a point in time when control transfers; customer acceptance clauses can defer recognition until acceptance.
  - Shipping and handling treated as fulfillment costs, not separate performance obligations; sales of goods typically lack multiple elements.
  - Revenue measured at expected consideration, excluding sales and value-added taxes; incidental contract costs expensed.
  - Allowances for returns, allowances, and price discounts recorded at recognition based on history and terms.
  - Warranty liabilities established and adjusted based on experience; not material as of December 31, 2022 and 2021.
  - Certain Telecommunications contracts (design, installation, training, software maintenance) recognized over time using straight-line or cost-based input methods; other revenue not material for 2020–2022.
- Contract assets and liabilities:
  - Contract assets (incremental obtain/fulfill costs) are insignificant; most fulfillment costs recorded as inventory, fixed assets, or intangibles; other fulfillment costs immaterial.
  - Contract liabilities include customer deposits (primarily Display products) and deferred revenue (primarily HSG); other advance payments are small and recorded in other accrued liabilities.
- Research and development:
  - Expensed as incurred; totals of $0.9B (2022), $0.8B (2021), and $1.0B (2020).
- Foreign currency:
  - Functional currency generally local; notable exception: a Taiwanese subsidiary uses Japanese yen.
  - Remeasurement gains/losses recognized in income: $130M gain (2022), $126M gain (2021), $37M loss (2020).

nodes.title: Contract Assets and Liabilities
nodes.heading: Contract Assets and Liabilities
nodes.start_phrase: Contract assets, such as incremental costs to obtain or fulfill contracts, are an insignificant component of Corning’s revenue recognition process.
nodes.summary:
- Revenue recognition: Predominantly at a point in time upon transfer of control for product sales; if customer acceptance is required and transfer of control can’t be objectively determined, revenue is recognized upon acceptance. Shipping and handling are fulfillment costs, not separate performance obligations. Consideration is measured net of sales and value-added taxes. Incidental contract costs are expensed. Estimates for returns, allowances, and price discounts reduce revenue; warranty liabilities are recorded based on experience and were not material at December 31, 2022 and 2021.
- Over-time revenue: Certain Telecommunications contracts (design, installation, training, software maintenance) are recognized over time using straight-line or input methods based on incurred/forecasted costs. Other revenue was not material for 2020–2022.
- Contract assets and liabilities: Contract assets (incremental costs to obtain/fulfill) are insignificant; most fulfillment costs are accounted for as inventory, fixed assets, or intangibles. Contract liabilities include customer deposits (primarily Display products) and deferred revenue (primarily HSG); other advance payments are recorded in other accrued liabilities and are not significant.
- Research and development: Expensed as incurred; $0.9 billion (2022), $0.8 billion (2021), $1.0 billion (2020).
- Foreign currency: Functional currency generally local; notable exception is a Taiwanese subsidiary using Japanese yen. Remeasurement gains/losses from non-functional currency transactions are recognized in income: gain of $130 million (2022), gain of $126 million (2021), loss of $37 million (2020).

nodes.title: Research and Development Costs
nodes.heading: Research and Development Costs
nodes.start_phrase: Research and development costs are charged to expense as incurred.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines Corning’s revenue recognition policies: product sales recognized at a point in time upon transfer of control; customer acceptance clauses may defer recognition; shipping and handling treated as fulfillment costs; revenue measured net of sales and value-added taxes; incidental contract costs expensed; allowances for returns, discounts, and warranties recorded at recognition based on experience, with warranty liabilities not material as of December 31, 2022 and 2021.
- Describes over-time revenue recognition for certain Telecommunications-related contracts (design, installation, training, and software maintenance) using straight-line or input methods based on incurred/forecasted costs; notes other revenue was not material for 2020–2022.
- Explains contract assets and liabilities: incremental costs to obtain/fulfill contracts are insignificant; most fulfillment costs are recorded as inventory, fixed assets, or intangibles; contract liabilities include customer deposits (primarily Display products), deferred revenue (primarily HSG), and other advances (not significant, recorded in other accrued liabilities).
- States research and development costs are expensed as incurred, totaling $0.9B (2022), $0.8B (2021), and $1.0B (2020).
- Details foreign currency policies: functional currency determined by economic factors (generally local currencies; a Taiwanese subsidiary uses JPY); remeasurement gains/losses recognized in income, with a gain of $130M (2022), gain of $126M (2021), and loss of $37M (2020).

nodes.title: Foreign Currency Translation and Transactions
nodes.heading: Foreign Currency Translation and Transactions
nodes.start_phrase: The determination of the functional currency for Corning’s foreign subsidiaries is made based on the appropriate economic factors.
nodes.summary:
- Revenue recognition: Primarily at a point in time upon transfer of control for product sales; customer acceptance clauses can defer recognition until acceptance. Sales generally do not include multiple elements. Shipping and handling are fulfillment costs, not separate performance obligations. Consideration excludes sales and value-added taxes; incidental contract costs are expensed. Estimates recorded for returns, allowances, and discounts; warranty liabilities based on experience and were not material at 12/31/22 and 12/31/21. Certain telecommunications-related services (design, installation, training, software maintenance) recognized over time using straight-line or input methods; other service revenue not material for 2020–2022.
- Contract assets and liabilities: Incremental costs to obtain/fulfill contracts are insignificant; most fulfillment costs are recorded as inventory, fixed assets, or intangibles. Contract liabilities include customer deposits (primarily Display products), deferred revenue (primarily HSG), and other small advance payments.
- Research and development: Expensed as incurred; $0.9B (2022), $0.8B (2021), $1.0B (2020).
- Foreign currency: Functional currency generally local; a Taiwanese subsidiary uses Japanese yen. Remeasurement gains/losses from non-functional currency transactions recognized in current income: gain $130M (2022), gain $126M (2021), loss $37M (2020). Translation of foreign subsidiaries recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss; long-term intra-entity FX also in AOCI. Cumulative translation gains/losses reclassified to earnings upon disposal/liquidation of foreign entities.
- Share-based compensation: Long-term incentive plans for employees and directors include restricted stock/RSUs (time-based), performance-based RSUs, options, and SARs. Expense based on grant-date fair value, recognized over requisite service for awards expected to vest; forfeiture rates based on long-term history and updated as needed. Expense allocated to cost of sales, SG&A, and R&D; related deferred tax benefits recognized during service with true-ups at vesting/exercise/forfeiture. Time-based awards valued at grant-date stock price; director awards expensed immediately. Performance-based RSUs earned on achievement of targets, typically vest over three years, valued at grant assuming target payout.

nodes.title: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.heading: Share-Based Compensation
nodes.start_phrase: Corning maintains long-term incentive plans (the “Plans”) for key employees and non-employee members of its Board of Directors.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency translation: Subsidiary balance sheets translated at period-end rates; income statements at average rates. Translation gains/losses recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI). Remeasurement of non-functional currency items goes to current earnings, except long-term intra-entity transactions, which go to AOCI. Upon sale or substantial liquidation of a foreign entity, accumulated translation adjustments are reclassified to earnings.
- Share-based compensation framework: Corning maintains long-term incentive plans for employees and non-employee directors, enabling grants of time-based and performance-based RS/RSUs, stock options, and SARs.
- Expense recognition and measurement: Awards measured at grant-date fair value and expensed over the requisite service period for awards expected to vest. Costs allocated to cost of sales, SG&A, and R&D. Forfeiture rates based on 15+ years of history, reassessed each period with cumulative catch-up adjustments. Awards with retirement provisions recognized over the expected performance period.
- Income tax effects: Deferred tax benefits recognized over the service period; differences between actual tax deductions and accrued tax benefits recognized in current income tax expense/benefit at vesting, exercise, forfeiture, or expiration.
- Time-based RS/RSUs: Payable in common stock upon vesting; fair value equals closing market price on grant date. For non-employee directors with no vesting terms, expense is recognized immediately.
- Performance-based RSUs: Earned upon achieving specified targets; typically vest over three years; fair value based on grant-date closing price assuming target payout.

nodes.title: Time-Based Restricted Stock and Restricted Stock Units
nodes.heading: Time-Based Restricted Stock and Restricted Stock Units
nodes.start_phrase: Time-based restricted stock and restricted stock units are issued by the Company on a discretionary basis, and are payable in shares of the Company’s common stock upon vesting.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency translation and remeasurement: balance sheet accounts translated at period-end rates; income statement accounts at average rates; translation gains/losses recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI). Remeasurement of non-functional currency items goes to current earnings, except long-term intra-entity transactions, which are included with translation adjustments in AOCI. Upon sale or substantial liquidation of a foreign entity, related accumulated translation gains/losses are reclassified to earnings.
- Share-based compensation framework: Corning’s long-term incentive plans cover key employees and non-employee directors and may include time-based restricted stock/RSUs, performance-based RSUs, stock options, and stock appreciation rights. Expense is allocated to cost of sales, SG&A, and R&D.
- Measurement and recognition: Compensation cost equals grant-date fair value and is recognized for awards expected to vest. The company estimates forfeitures using 15+ years of historical data, reassesses each reporting period, and records cumulative adjustments for changes. For awards with retirement provisions to retirement-eligible employees, expense is recognized over the expected performance period.
- Income tax effects: A deferred tax benefit is recorded during the service period; at vesting, exercise, forfeiture, or expiration, differences from the accrued tax benefit are recognized in current income tax expense/benefit.
- Time-based restricted stock/RSUs: Payable in shares upon vesting; fair value based on the closing stock price on the grant date. For director awards with no vesting terms, expense is recognized immediately.
- Performance-based RSUs: Earned upon achievement of specified targets; payable in shares and typically vest over three years. Fair value is based on the grant-date closing stock price, assuming target payout.

nodes.title: Performance-Based Restricted Stock Units
nodes.heading: Performance-Based Restricted Stock Units
nodes.start_phrase: Performance-based restricted stock units are earned upon the achievement of certain targets and are payable in shares of the Company’s common stock upon vesting, typically over a three year period.
nodes.summary:
- Foreign currency translation and remeasurement: functional currency balance sheets translated at period-end rates; income statements at average rates; translation gains/losses to accumulated other comprehensive loss (AOCI); remeasurement gains/losses to earnings except long-term intra-entity items to AOCI; reclassification to earnings upon disposal/liquidation of foreign operations.
- Share-based compensation policy: awards under long-term incentive plans (restricted stock/units, performance units, stock options, SARs); expense allocated to cost of sales, SG&A, and R&D; fair value measured at grant; recognition based on expected vesting with estimated forfeitures and periodic reassessment; retirement-eligible provisions; deferred tax benefits during service period and true-up at vesting/exercise/forfeiture.
- Time-based restricted stock/RSUs: fair value at grant date stock price; immediate expense for non-employee directors due to no vesting terms.
- Performance-based RSUs: earned on achievement of targets, typically vest over three years; fair value based on grant date stock price assuming target payout.
- Stock options: non-qualified and incentive options granted at grant-date market price; vest in tranches over 1–5 years; 10-year term; non-substantive vesting approach; fair value via multiple-point Black-Scholes using blended volatility (implied, recent, 15-year historical), risk-free zero-coupon Treasury matching expected term, expected term from historical exercise behavior and life cycles, and forfeiture rates.
- Cash and cash equivalents: highly liquid investments with maturities ≤3 months; carrying value approximates fair value.
- Supplemental cash flow disclosures: non-cash capex accruals; cash paid for interest and income taxes; note on capitalized interest amounts included in PP&E.
- Trade accounts receivable: allowance for doubtful accounts reflects estimated lifetime credit losses using historical write-offs and industry default expectations with specific reserves as needed; no significant off-balance-sheet credit exposure.
- Inventories: stated at lower of cost or net realizable value using FIFO.
- Property, plant, and equipment: recorded at cost; straight-line depreciation (buildings/improvements 10–40 years; equipment 2–20 years; precious metals treated separately); capitalization of interest during active construction and amortization over asset lives.

nodes.title: Stock Options
nodes.heading: Stock Options
nodes.start_phrase: Corning’s stock option plans provide non-qualified and incentive stock options to purchase authorized but unissued common shares, or treasury shares, at the closing market price on the grant date and generally become exercisable in tranches from one year to five years from the grant date.
nodes.summary:
- Stock options: Plan terms (non-qualified and incentive options granted at grant-date market price; vesting over 1–5 years; 10-year maximum term). Vesting considered complete when continued service is no longer required (non-substantive vesting period). Fair value estimated using a multiple-point Black-Scholes model with assumptions for expected volatility (blended implied/recent/15-year historical), dividend yield, risk-free rate (zero-coupon U.S. Treasury matching expected term), expected term (based on historical exercises and current vesting), and forfeiture rates.
- Cash and cash equivalents: Highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less; carrying amounts approximate fair value. Supplemental cash flow data for 2020–2022: non-cash accruals for capital expenditures; cash paid for interest and income taxes; and capitalized interest included in PP&E each year.
- Trade accounts receivable: Allowance for doubtful accounts reflects estimated lifetime expected credit losses based on historical write-offs, industry default expectations, and specific customer risks; no significant off-balance-sheet credit exposure.
- Inventories: Stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value using FIFO.
- Property, plant and equipment: Recorded at cost (including precious metals); straight-line depreciation (buildings/improvements 10–40 years; equipment 2–20 years, excluding precious metals). Interest on borrowings is capitalized during construction of major projects, added to asset cost, and amortized over asset lives.

nodes.title: Cash and Cash Equivalents
nodes.heading: Cash and Cash Equivalents
nodes.start_phrase: Cash equivalents consist of highly liquid investments that are readily convertible into cash.
nodes.summary:
The excerpt continues Corning’s Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, covering:
- Stock options: Non-qualified and incentive awards granted at market price, vesting in tranches over 1–5 years, with a maximum 10-year term and vesting defined under the non-substantive vesting period approach. Fair value is measured using a multiple-point Black-Scholes model with assumptions for expected volatility (blended implied/recent/historical, including a 15-year lookback), dividend yield, risk-free U.S. Treasury rates matched to expected term, expected term based on historical exercise behavior adjusted for current vesting and partial life cycles, and forfeiture rates.
- Cash and cash equivalents: Highly liquid investments with maturities of three months or less; carrying values approximate fair value. Supplemental cash flow details (in millions) for 2022/2021/2020: non-cash accruals for capital expenditures $414/$357/$231; cash paid for interest $275/$287/$298 (including capitalized interest of $48/$36/$58); and income taxes paid (net) $426/$377/$220.
- Trade accounts receivable: Allowance for doubtful accounts reflects estimated lifetime credit losses based on historical write-offs and expected industry default rates, with specific allowances as needed; no significant off-balance-sheet credit exposure.
- Inventories: Stated at lower of cost or net realizable value using FIFO.
- Property, plant and equipment: Recorded at cost (including precious metals); straight-line depreciation with useful lives of 10–40 years for buildings/improvements and 2–20 years for equipment (excluding precious metals). Interest on borrowings is capitalized during active construction and amortized over asset lives.

nodes.title: Trade Accounts Receivable, net of Doubtful Accounts
nodes.heading: Trade Accounts Receivable, net of Doubtful Accounts
nodes.start_phrase: The allowance for doubtful accounts is based on the best estimate of the amount of probable lifetime credit losses in existing accounts receivable.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines stock option accounting: Corning grants non-qualified and incentive options at market price, typically vesting over 1–5 years with a maximum 10-year term; applies the non-substantive vesting period approach for vesting. Options are valued using a multiple-point Black-Scholes model with assumptions for expected volatility (blended short-term implied, recent term-matched, and 15-year historical), dividend yield, risk-free zero-coupon Treasury rates matched to expected term, expected term based on historical exercise behavior and current vesting, and forfeiture rates.
- Defines cash and cash equivalents as highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less; carrying amounts approximate fair value. Provides supplemental cash flow disclosures (2020–2022): non-cash capital expenditure accruals; cash paid for interest and income taxes; and interest capitalized into property, plant, and equipment.
- Describes trade accounts receivable policy: allowance reflects best estimate of probable lifetime credit losses using historical write-offs and expected industry default rates, with specific allowances for known customer issues; no significant off-balance-sheet credit exposure.
- States inventory accounting: lower of cost or net realizable value, using FIFO.
- Details property, plant, and equipment: recorded at cost (including precious metals); straight-line depreciation with useful lives generally 10–40 years for buildings/improvements and 2–20 years for equipment; capitalization of interest during construction and subsequent amortization over asset lives.

nodes.title: Inventories
nodes.heading: Inventories
nodes.start_phrase: Inventories are stated at the lower of cost or net realizable value using the first-in, first-out method.
nodes.summary:
- Continuation of Summary of Significant Accounting Policies focused on equity compensation and key balance sheet items.
- Stock options: Plans grant non-qualified and incentive options at market closing price on grant date; vest in tranches over 1–5 years; maximum term 10 years; vesting defined under a non-substantive vesting period approach. Fair value estimated using a multiple-point Black-Scholes model with assumptions for expected volatility (blended implied/recent/15-year historical), dividend yield, risk-free rate (zero-coupon U.S. Treasury matched to expected term), expected term (based on historical exercise behavior and current vesting/partial life cycles), and forfeiture rates.
- Cash and cash equivalents: Highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less; carrying amounts approximate fair value. Includes supplemental cash flow disclosures for non-cash capital expenditure accruals and cash paid for interest and income taxes, with a portion of interest capitalized to property, plant and equipment.
- Trade accounts receivable: Allowance for doubtful accounts reflects lifetime expected credit losses based on historical write-offs and industry default rates; specific reserves recorded for known customer credit issues; no significant off-balance-sheet credit exposure.
- Inventories: Carried at lower of cost or net realizable value using FIFO.
- Property, plant, and equipment: Recorded at cost; depreciated on a straight-line basis (buildings/improvements generally 10–40 years; equipment 2–20 years; precious metals addressed separately); interest on borrowings capitalized during active construction and amortized over asset lives.

nodes.title: Property, Plant and Equipment, Net of Accumulated Depreciation
nodes.heading: Property, Plant and Equipment, Net of Accumulated Depreciation
nodes.start_phrase: Land, buildings and equipment, including precious metals, are recorded at cost.
nodes.summary:
- Part of Corning’s Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, detailing:
  - Stock options: plan terms (non-qualified and incentive options), grant pricing, vesting (1–5 years), 10-year max term, and valuation using a multiple-point Black-Scholes model with blended volatility, dividend yield, risk-free rate (zero-coupon U.S. Treasury), expected term, and forfeiture assumptions.
  - Cash and cash equivalents: definition (maturities ≤3 months) and fair value; supplemental cash flow disclosures for 2020–2022 (accruals for capital expenditures; cash paid for interest including capitalized portions; and income taxes).
  - Trade accounts receivable: allowance based on lifetime expected credit losses using historical write-offs, industry default rates, and specific customer assessments; no significant off-balance-sheet credit exposure.
  - Inventories: measured at lower of cost or net realizable value using FIFO.
  - Property, plant, and equipment: recorded at cost; straight-line depreciation with stated useful life ranges; interest capitalization during construction; useful life ranges by asset type; special treatment of precious-metal components (not depreciated; depletion expense for physical loss; held only to support operations).
  - Leases: recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for terms >12 months; use of incremental borrowing rate or implicit rate; combining lease and non-lease components; treatment of renewal/termination options; expense recognition for operating vs. finance leases; not a significant lessor.
  - Impairment of long-lived assets: trigger-based recoverability tests using undiscounted cash flows; fair value measurement via income approach (including disposition and precious metals) if not recoverable; assessment at lowest identifiable cash-flow level; quarterly monitoring; note of a 2020 impairment tied to Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.heading: Leases
nodes.start_phrase: Corning leases certain real estate, vehicles and equipment from third parties, which are classified as operating or finance leases.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines useful life ranges for equipment categories: computer hardware/software (3–7 years), manufacturing equipment (2–15), furniture/fixtures (5–10), and transportation equipment (3–20).
- Explains treatment of precious metals embedded in manufacturing equipment: not depreciated due to minimal physical loss and long useful life; physical losses are expensed as depletion based on actual units lost; metals are held solely to support operations, not for trading.
- Describes lease accounting: recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities at commencement for leases over 12 months; measurement using present value of lease payments with the incremental borrowing rate or implicit rate; election to combine lease and non-lease components; inclusion of reasonably certain renewal/termination options; straight-line expense for operating leases; effective interest and straight-line amortization for finance leases; no significant lessor activities.
- Details impairment policy for long-lived assets: quarterly assessment for indicators; recoverability test using undiscounted cash flows including eventual disposition; if not recoverable, fair value measured via an income approach considering future cash flows and, when applicable, precious metals’ market value; impairment recognized for the excess of carrying value over fair value; impairment recorded in 2020 related to R&D reprioritization within Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses.

nodes.title: Impairment of Long-Lived Assets
nodes.heading: Impairment of Long-Lived Assets
nodes.start_phrase: The recoverability of long-lived assets, such as property, plant and equipment and intangible assets, is reviewed when events or changes in circumstances occur that indicate the carrying value of the asset or asset group may not be recoverable.
nodes.summary:
- Asset useful lives: Specifies depreciation ranges for computer hardware/software (3–7 years), manufacturing equipment (2–15), furniture/fixtures (5–10), and transportation equipment (3–20). Precious metal components in manufacturing equipment are not depreciated; physical losses are expensed as depletion based on units lost and the metals are held solely to support operations.
- Lease accounting: Recognizes right-of-use assets and lease liabilities for leases over 12 months using the incremental borrowing or implicit rate; combines lease and non-lease components; includes reasonably certain renewal/termination options; straight-line expense for operating leases and interest/amortization for finance leases; no significant lessor arrangements.
- Impairment of long-lived assets: Trigger-based recoverability tests using undiscounted cash flows; if not recoverable, fair value measured via income approach considering future cash flows, terminal value, and precious metals; assessed at the lowest independent cash flow level; quarterly review; notes a 2020 impairment related to Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses.
- Goodwill: Assigned to reporting units; reviewed quarterly for indicators with a detailed quantitative discounted cash flow test every three years; impairment recognized if fair value is below carrying value; 2020 quantitative test showed fair values significantly exceeded carrying values.
- Government assistance: Cash incentives for capital projects recognized when compliance with conditions is probable; reduce asset cost or offset related expenses; 2022 impacts not material; year-end 2022 balances include $92 million in other accrued liabilities and $74 million in other liabilities, mainly for Display and Pharmaceutical Technologies, expected to be realized in 1–2 years.
- Environmental liabilities: Accrued when probable and estimable based on most likely costs, laws, and experience; considers share among responsible parties and their ability to pay; minimum of a reasonable range accrued if no better point estimate; insurance receivables recorded when reimbursement is virtually certain; acknowledges inherent uncertainty and potential for additional future costs.
- Equity method investments: Balances of $261 million (2022) and $264 million (2021); sales to affiliates were $228 million (2022), $312 million (2021), and $253 million (2020).

nodes.title: Goodwill
nodes.heading: Goodwill
nodes.start_phrase: Goodwill is the excess of cost of an acquired entity over the amounts assigned to assets acquired and liabilities assumed in a business combination.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines Corning’s accounting policy for goodwill: assigned to specific reporting units; assessed for impairment quarterly upon indicators and via a comprehensive quantitative test every three years; quantitative test uses an income approach (discounted cash flows with terminal value); impairment recognized if fair value is below carrying value; last quantitative test in 2020 showed fair values significantly exceeded carrying amounts.
- Describes accounting for government assistance: cash incentives for capital projects recorded as liabilities when compliance with conditions is probable; incentives reduce the cost of related property, plant and equipment or offset related expenses in the income statement. Notes that 2022 incentives recognized were not material to results; at December 31, 2022, $92 million in other accrued liabilities and $74 million in other liabilities, largely for Display Technologies and Pharmaceutical Technologies projects, expected to be realized over 1–2 years.
- Details environmental liability recognition: accruals recorded when probable and reasonably estimable; based on site-specific facts, laws, and prior experience; considers proportionate share at multi-party sites and other parties’ ability to pay; if no best estimate within a range, accrues the minimum undiscounted amount; recognizes insurance receivables when reimbursement is virtually certain; acknowledges uncertainty that could lead to additional future costs.
- Summarizes equity method investments: carrying value of $261 million and $264 million at December 31, 2022 and 2021, respectively; sales to affiliates of $228 million (2022), $312 million (2021), and $253 million (2020).

nodes.title: Government Assistance
nodes.heading: Government Assistance
nodes.start_phrase: The Company receives government assistance, typically in the form of cash incentives primarily for capital expansion projects.
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill: Defines goodwill and its assignment to reporting units; outlines impairment testing—ongoing qualitative reviews quarterly and a detailed quantitative discounted cash flow test every three years; records a loss if fair value is below carrying value; the 2020 quantitative test showed fair values significantly exceeded carrying amounts.

- Government assistance: Describes recognition of cash incentives as liabilities when compliance with conditions is probable; incentives reduce the cost of property, plant and equipment or offset related expenses in income; 2022 recognized amounts were not material; at December 31, 2022, $92 million in other accrued liabilities and $74 million in other liabilities, primarily for Display Technologies and Pharmaceutical Technologies, expected to be realized over 1–2 years.

- Environmental liabilities: Accrues costs when probable and reasonably estimable, based on site-specific facts, laws, and experience; considers proportionate shares among responsible parties and uses the minimum in a range if no best estimate; records insurance receivables when reimbursement is virtually certain; notes inherent uncertainty that may lead to additional future costs.

- Equity method investments: Reports balances of $261 million (2022) and $264 million (2021); discloses sales to affiliated companies of $228 million (2022), $312 million (2021), and $253 million (2020).

nodes.title: Environmental Liabilities
nodes.heading: Environmental Liabilities
nodes.start_phrase: The Company accrues for its environmental investigation, remediation, operating and maintenance costs when it is probable that a liability has been incurred and the amount can be reasonably estimated.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines Corning’s accounting policy for goodwill: assigned to specific reporting units (operating segments or one level below), monitored quarterly for impairment indicators, with a comprehensive quantitative impairment test every three years as a validation of the qualitative review. The quantitative test uses a discounted cash flow income approach; the 2020 test showed fair values significantly exceeded carrying values.
- Describes accounting for government assistance, primarily cash incentives for capital expansion: recorded as liabilities when compliance with conditions is probable; incentives reduce the cost of property, plant and equipment or offset related expenses in the income statement. For 2022, recognized impacts were not material; year-end balances included $92 million in other accrued liabilities and $74 million in other liabilities, mainly for Display Technologies and Pharmaceutical Technologies, expected to be realized over 1–2 years.
- Details environmental liability recognition: accrues probable and reasonably estimable investigation, remediation, and O&M costs based on site-specific facts, laws, experience, and proportionate responsibility; records the minimum undiscounted amount when no estimate in a range is more likely; recognizes insurance receivables when reimbursement is virtually certain; notes inherent uncertainty that could increase future costs.
- Summarizes equity method investments: carrying amounts of $261 million (2022) and $264 million (2021); sales to affiliated companies of $228 million (2022), $312 million (2021), and $253 million (2020).

nodes.title: Equity Method Investments
nodes.heading: Equity Method Investments
nodes.start_phrase: As of December 31, 2022 and 2021, Corning had investments in affiliated companies accounted for by the equity method totaling $261 million and $264 million, respectively.
nodes.summary:
The partial document outlines key accounting policies and related disclosures for Corning, focusing on:

- Goodwill: Defined as purchase price excess over net assets in business combinations, assigned to reporting units. Impairment is assessed quarterly via a qualitative review, with a detailed quantitative DCF-based test performed every three years as a validation (last in 2020, fair values significantly exceeded carrying values). Losses are recognized if fair value is below carrying value.

- Government assistance: Cash incentives, primarily for capital projects, are recognized as liabilities when compliance with conditions is probable. Incentives reduce the cost of property, plant and equipment or offset related expenses in income. For 2022, recognized amounts were not material. At December 31, 2022, $92 million was in other accrued liabilities and $74 million in other liabilities, largely tied to Display Technologies and Pharmaceutical Technologies, expected to be realized over 1–2 years.

- Environmental liabilities: Accrued when probable and reasonably estimable, based on most likely costs considering facts, laws, experience, and proportionate shares at multi-party sites. If no amount in a range is more likely, the minimum is accrued. Insurance recoveries are recorded when virtually certain. Actual outcomes may vary and lead to additional future costs.

- Equity method investments: Balances were $261 million (2022) and $264 million (2021). Sales to affiliates were $228 million (2022), $312 million (2021), and $253 million (2020). Investments are reviewed for impairment; if recovery is not probable, other-than-temporary impairments are recorded to fair value. Other non-consolidated equity investments are measured at fair value through net income or under the measurement alternative (cost adjusted for impairment/observable changes); such holdings were not material in 2022 and 2021.

- Employee retirement plans: Includes defined benefit pensions and postretirement health/life plans. Costs depend on economic and demographic assumptions. Pension expense comprises quarterly ongoing costs (service, interest, expected return, amortization of prior service cost) and annual fourth-quarter mark-to-market gains/losses outside a 10% corridor; interim remeasurements occur upon significant events. Postretirement costs include ongoing components with actuarial gains/losses recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and amortized if outside the corridor.

- Income taxes: Uses the asset-liability method for deferred taxes, with valuation allowances when realization is not more likely than not. Uncertain tax positions are recognized at the highest cumulative benefit more likely than not to be sustained; adjustments occur upon filing or new information. Liabilities for unrecognized tax benefits (including interest and penalties) are recorded in other accrued and long-term liabilities, with impacts in income tax expense. Discrete events are recognized in the period incurred. The company generally intends to indefinitely reinvest foreign earnings for entities lacking distributable earnings/capability, where reinvestment is intended, with non-controlling interests, with accumulated deficits, or where distributions would incur significant net costs.

nodes.title: Employee Retirement Plans
nodes.heading: Employee Retirement Plans
nodes.start_phrase: Corning offers employee retirement plans consisting of defined benefit pension plans covering certain domestic and international employees and postretirement plans that provide health care and life insurance benefits for eligible retirees and dependents.
nodes.summary:
- Equity method investments: periodic impairment reviews; fair value measured via discounted cash flows or other methods when indicators exist; other-than-temporary impairments recorded in earnings; non-consolidated, non-equity-method investments measured at fair value through net income or under the measurement alternative (cost minus impairment plus/minus observable price changes); such investments were immaterial at December 31, 2022 and 2021.
- Employee retirement plans: defined benefit pension and postretirement health/life plans; costs depend on economic/demographic assumptions (interest rates, expected asset returns, compensation growth, healthcare trends, mortality/turnover); pension costs include ongoing quarterly elements (service cost, interest cost, expected return, amortization of prior service cost) and annual Q4 mark-to-market outside a 10% corridor (of the greater of benefit obligation or market-related asset value); interim remeasurements for curtailments, settlements, or significant plan changes.
- Postretirement benefit plans: quarterly recognition of service and interest costs, amortization of prior service costs, and actuarial gains/losses; actuarial gains/losses recognized in accumulated other comprehensive loss annually and amortized over the average remaining service period when outside the corridor.
- Income taxes: asset and liability method; recognition of deferred tax assets/liabilities for temporary differences and carryforwards; valuation allowances when realization is not more-likely-than-not; uncertain tax positions measured using the highest cumulative benefit more-likely-than-not to be realized; adjustments recorded upon filing or new information; unrecognized tax benefits (with penalties/interest) recorded in accrued and long-term liabilities and in income tax expense; discrete items recognized in the period of occurrence; policy to indefinitely reinvest certain foreign earnings based on ability/intention, non-controlling interests, accumulated deficits, or significant repatriation costs.

nodes.title: Income Taxes
nodes.heading: Income Taxes
nodes.start_phrase: The Company accounts for income taxes using the asset and liability method.
nodes.summary:
- Equity method investments: Periodic impairment assessments based on performance and impairment indicators; fair value measured via discounted cash flows or other methods; other-than-temporary impairments recognized in earnings with carrying value reduced to fair value.
- Other equity investments: Non-consolidated, non-equity-method holdings measured at fair value with changes in net income; use of the measurement alternative for investments without readily determinable fair values (cost less impairment plus/minus observable price changes); balances not material as of Dec 31, 2022 and 2021.
- Employee retirement plans: Defined benefit pension and postretirement health/life plans; costs depend on economic and demographic assumptions. Pension cost elements include quarterly service/interest/expected return/amortization and annual mark-to-market outside a 10% corridor (with interim remeasurements for curtailments/settlements/plan changes). Postretirement costs include service/interest and amortization of prior service and actuarial amounts, with actuarial gains/losses recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and amortized if outside the corridor.
- Income taxes: Asset and liability method; recognition of deferred tax assets/liabilities for basis differences and carryforwards; valuation allowances when realization is not more likely than not. Uncertain tax positions measured as the highest cumulative benefit more likely than not to be realized; changes recognized upon filing or new information; liabilities (including penalties/interest) recorded in accrued and long-term liabilities and in income tax expense. Discrete items (e.g., audit settlements, law changes) recognized in the period of occurrence. Policy to indefinitely reinvest certain foreign earnings based on specified criteria.
- Fair value measurements: Recurring fair value for major financial assets/liabilities; nonrecurring for impaired assets (long-lived assets, goodwill, equity method investments, other investments, AROs). Fair value based on exit price in principal or most advantageous market using market participant assumptions. Three-level hierarchy: Level 1 (quoted prices), Level 2 (other observable inputs), Level 3 (significant unobservable inputs).
- Derivative instruments: Use of FX forwards/options and derivatives bifurcated from precious metals lease contracts to manage currency and precious metals price exposures. All derivatives at fair value on the balance sheet. Cash flow hedges’ changes recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified to earnings with the hedged item. Fair value hedges’ changes (excluding time value) recognized in other income (expense). Non-designated derivatives’ changes recognized in translated earnings contract gain (loss), net, and other income (expense).
- New accounting standards: Adoption of the FASB government assistance disclosure standard resulted in no material impact; recently issued standards are not expected to materially affect the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.heading: Fair Value Measurements
nodes.start_phrase: Major categories of financial assets and liabilities, including short-term investments, other assets and derivatives, are measured at fair value on a recurring basis.
nodes.summary:
- The section outlines Corning’s policies for fair value measurements of financial assets and liabilities. It distinguishes between items measured at fair value on a recurring basis (e.g., short-term investments, other assets, derivatives) and on a nonrecurring basis when impaired (e.g., long-lived assets, goodwill, equity method and other investments, asset retirement obligations).
- Fair value is defined as the exit price in an orderly transaction, determined using the principal or most advantageous market and market-participant assumptions, including considerations of inherent risk, transfer restrictions, and non-performance risk.
- A three-level fair value hierarchy is described: Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (other observable inputs), and Level 3 (unobservable inputs).
- Derivative instruments policy covers use of foreign exchange forwards and options to manage currency risk, and derivatives bifurcated from precious metals lease contracts to manage exposure to metal price changes.
- Accounting for derivatives: all recorded at fair value on the balance sheet; cash flow hedge gains/losses deferred in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified to earnings when hedged items affect results; fair value hedge changes (excluding time value) recognized in current earnings within other income (expense), net; non-designated derivatives recognized in translated earnings contract gain (loss), net and other income (expense), net.
- New accounting standards: disclosure of government assistance under ASU 2021-10 is noted; adoption of related guidance (referenced as ASU 2020-10) had no material impact; newly issued standards are not expected to materially affect the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: Derivative Instruments
nodes.heading: Derivative Instruments
nodes.start_phrase: The Company enters into a variety of foreign exchange forward contracts and foreign exchange option contracts to manage the exposure to fluctuations in foreign exchange rates.
nodes.summary:
- Continues the Summary of Significant Accounting Policies, covering Fair Value Measurements, Derivative Instruments, and New Accounting Standards.
- Fair value measurements:
  - Defines fair value as the exit price in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date, considering principal/most advantageous market and market participant assumptions (e.g., inherent risk, transfer restrictions, non-performance risk).
  - Uses a three-level hierarchy: Level 1 (quoted prices in active markets), Level 2 (other observable inputs), Level 3 (unobservable inputs).
  - Recurring fair value items include short-term investments, other assets, and derivatives.
  - Nonrecurring fair value measurements apply upon impairment to long-lived assets, goodwill, equity method investments, other investments, and asset retirement obligations.
- Derivative instruments:
  - Utilizes foreign exchange forwards and options to manage currency risk, and derivatives bifurcated from precious metals lease contracts to manage price risk of leased metals.
  - All derivatives recorded at fair value on the balance sheet.
  - Hedge accounting:
    - Cash flow hedges: fair value changes recorded in accumulated other comprehensive loss and reclassified to earnings (sales, cost of sales, or other income/expense) when the hedged item affects income.
    - Fair value hedges: changes (excluding time value) recognized in other income (expense), net.
    - Non-designated derivatives: changes recognized in translated earnings contract gain (loss), net and other income (expense), net.
- New accounting standards:
  - Notes FASB ASU 2021-10 on disclosures of government assistance; adoption did not have a material impact.
  - Recently issued standards are not expected to materially affect the consolidated financial statements.

nodes.title: HSG Transactions and Acquisitions

Accounted for under the acquisition method without net cash consideration; fair value determined via income approach (16.5% discount rate, 0% terminal growth). Corning recognized a $498 million pre-tax gain on its previously held equity investment upon consolidation. From that date, HSG results are consolidated within Hemlock and Emerging Growth Businesses; HSG’s 2020 net income impact was not material.

- Employee Retirement Plans
  - Defined benefit pension and postretirement health/life plans; contributions to international pensions were $24 million in 2021; planned 2023 contributions of $49 million to international plans. Retiree medical “cap” set at 120% of 2005 contributions (reached for post-65 in 2008 and pre-65 in 2010); employees hired/re-hired on/after 1/1/2007 pay 100% of retiree medical cost though remain eligible.

OCI reflects actuarial and prior service cost changes.
  - Assumptions and methodology: discount rates derived from a high-quality corporate bond yield curve; mortality based on PRI-2012 tables with MP-2020 improvements; 2022 discount rates rose materially (e.g., domestic pension 5.50% vs 2.87% in 2021; postretirement 5.58% vs 2.99%). Health care trend assumption (2022): 7.00% pre-65 / 4.25% post-65, grading to 5% (ultimate) by 2031.
  - Plan assets and risks: target allocation ~40% equities / 60% bonds with long-duration fixed income to manage interest rate risk. Domestic plan assets at 12/31/22 totaled $2,688 million with small Level 3 exposure (~1%) in private equity/real estate; international plan assets $381 million including insurance contracts and mortgages. Credit risk concentrated in AA- average rated bonds (54% of domestic assets); limited liquidity risk from Level 3 holdings.
  - Expected benefit payments (in millions): next five years for domestic pensions ~$242–$265 annually; international pensions ~$27–$38; postretirement ~$29–$31; 2028–2032 totals $1,393 (domestic), $213 (international), $156 (postretirement).

nodes.title: Commitments, Contingencies and Guarantees
nodes.heading: 13. Commitments, Contingencies and Guarantees
nodes.start_phrase: The Company is required, at the time a guarantee is issued, to recognize a liability for the fair value or market value of the obligation it assumes.
nodes.summary:
- Covers Note 13 (Commitments, Contingencies and Guarantees) and Note 14 (Hedging Activities) from Corning’s financial statements.
- Guarantees: Corning recognizes liabilities at fair value when issued; typically provides limited third‑party guarantees (standby letters of credit, performance bonds, milestone-based purchase price adjustments). Guarantees are varied, not individually significant, and expected largely to expire unfunded.
- Purchase commitments: Binding obligations primarily for raw materials and energy take‑or‑pay contracts, with commitments as of Dec 31, 2022 of $230m (<1 year), $212m (1–3 years), $102m (3–5 years), and $453m (5+ years).
- Litigation/environmental/indemnifications: Corning faces routine lawsuits and claims; management deems the likelihood of a material adverse effect to be remote.
- Dow Corning Chapter 11–related indemnity: Post-2016 realignment, Corning agreed to indemnify Dow for 50% of non‑ordinary course, pre‑closing liabilities exceeding Dow Corning’s May 31, 2016 reserves, subject to conditions and limits; not expected to be material.
- Dow Corning environmental claims: Dow notified Corning in 2019 of environmental losses at multiple sites; Corning may indemnify up to 50%, subject to limits. As of Dec 31, 2022, a liability is probable but the reserve is not material.
- Environmental matters: Corning is a potentially responsible party at 19 hazardous waste sites; accrued undiscounted environmental cleanup and related litigation liabilities of ~$109m at Dec 31, 2022 (vs. $55m in 2021); management considers the reserve a reasonable estimate.
- Hedging activities focus on mitigating foreign currency risk, primarily in JPY, KRW, TWD, CNY, EUR, and GBP, using OTC forwards and options aligned with underlying exposures.
- Counterparty risk is minimized via a diversified set of highly rated financial institutions; no collateral is required by either party; Corning uses the Dodd‑Frank end‑user clearing exception.
- Designated cash flow hedges: FX forwards with gross notional of $419m at Dec 31, 2022 ($780m in 2021), maturities through 2024; $20m pre‑tax gain expected to be reclassified to earnings within 12 months.
- Designated fair value hedges: Embedded derivatives in leased precious metals hedged; time value excluded and amortized. Carrying amount of leased precious metals pool was $278m in 2022 ($107m in 2021), including cumulative fair value losses of $95m in 2022 ($5m in 2021).
- Hedge effectiveness assessed via regression or critical terms match initially, with quarterly qualitative assessments thereafter.
- Undesignated hedges: FX forwards and options used to offset economic currency risks on monetary items and translated earnings, notably for JPY (maturities through 2024) and KRW (through 2026), and also TWD, CNY, and EUR.

nodes.title: Hedging Activities
nodes.heading: 14. Hedging Activities
nodes.start_phrase: Corning is primarily exposed to foreign currency risks due to fluctuations in exchange rates.
nodes.summary:
- Focus: Corning’s hedging activities (Section 14) and fair value measurements (Section 15).
- Risk exposure: Primarily foreign currency risk (JPY, KRW, TWD, CNY, EUR, GBP); also precious metals price risk tied to leased metals.
- Instruments and strategy: Use of OTC foreign exchange forwards and options; maturities aligned with underlying exposures; diversified, highly rated counterparties; no collateral posting; elected Dodd-Frank end-user clearing exception.
- Designated hedges:
  - Cash flow hedges (FX forwards) for forecasted sales/purchases; gross notional $419m (2022) vs $780m (2021), maturities through 2024; hedge results deferred in AOCI; ~$20m pre-tax gain expected to be reclassified to earnings within 12 months (as of 12/31/22).
  - Fair value hedges for precious metals leases (maturities through 2025) via bifurcated embedded derivatives; changes recognized in earnings; time value excluded and amortized; leased metals carrying amount $278m (2022) vs $107m (2021) including cumulative fair value losses of $95m (2022) vs $5m (2021).
  - Hedge effectiveness assessed via regression or critical terms match initially; ongoing quarterly qualitative assessments.
- Undesignated hedges: FX forwards and options to economically hedge monetary assets/liabilities and translated earnings; significant focus on JPY (maturities through 2024) and KRW (through 2026).
- Translated earnings program: Total gross notional $7.5b (2022) vs $8.9b (2021); mix of average rate forwards (JPY, KRW, other) and options (JPY, prior-year multi-currency baskets, zero-cost collars where only one leg can be exercised).
- Accounting and results:
  - Derivative fair values recorded as assets/liabilities; undesignated changes recognized in “translated earnings contract gain (loss), net.”
  - Total derivative notional $10.2b (2022) vs $13.5b (2021); derivative assets $678m and liabilities $191m (2022).
  - AOCI included $19m accumulated derivative gain (2022) vs $52m (2021).
  - 2022 P&L effects: designated hedges—$52m gain in OCI; $81m net reclassified to income (net sales, cost of sales, other income/expense). Undesignated hedges—$397m gain (FX contracts $46m; translated earnings $351m). 2020 de-designation note of $14m loss previously reclassified.
- Fair value measurements (Section 15): Derivative assets/liabilities primarily Level 2; 12/31/22 balances—other current assets $505m (mostly Level 2), other assets $225m (mostly Level 2), other accrued liabilities $174m (Level 2), other liabilities $34m (Level 2). No significant nonrecurring fair value measurements in 2022 or 2021.
